issues.title: Reader Recomendo: 24 favorites
issues.html:
For our first Reader Recomendo, we asked you to send us one thing you love that more people should know about. More than 100 of you did. Kevin, Mark and I read every one, and these are our favorites. The rest of the reader picks are on our full list page. Thank you for sharing your favorite things with us. — CD


Around the House

No more sheet burritos
We have a large household, so washing bedding is a nonstop routine, and in our part of Canada line drying isn’t an option for most of the year. The dryer is, but the dryer means multiple cycles of untangling the wads that our sheets would inevitably burrito themselves into. Dryer balls didn’t help. Then I found the Wad-Free Bed Sheet Detangler. It seemed pricey for an unflashy, oddly shaped piece of plastic, but it worked spectacularly well. You’ll need the instructions to make a sort of parachute with your sheet. Now our sheets dry in a single cycle. We save electricity, time and a few nerve cells. One of the best household products we’ve ever bought. — Valentin from Quispamsis, Canada

Back-saver shovel handle
We shovel a lot of snow in New Hampshire, and our backs know it. This Back-Saving Tool Handle clamps onto any style of shovel and really saves my lower back. I can shovel even heavy snow now without hours of back pain later. It’s rugged too. I’ve used mine through six winters, and it’s still solid and doesn’t need constant tightening. — Tammy in New Hampshire

Every job needs The Muji
Nearly every home project I’ve done for the last 25 years has involved this small Muji Driver Set. The sturdy plastic case holds four Phillips heads, three flat heads and a surprisingly sharp awl, and the handle works straight or flipped sideways for extra leverage. It’s about the size of a fat deck of cards, so it lives in our utility drawer instead of the toolbox, and it replaces bigger tools 75% of the time. Because it’s easy to grab, small things get fixed right away. We call it “The Muji,” and at under $10 we gift it often. — Serena Worthington

The $5 package opener
In 2026, excess packaging is impossible to outrun. The Slice Safety Cutter is featherlight and wildly effective. It opens boxes, plastic wrap, clamshells and letters with almost no pressure, and the ceramic blade is designed so you can’t cut yourself. It has replaced several knives and scissors in my home, and the magnet means it lives on my fridge and never gets lost. I’ve given away more than 30 of these over the last four years for housewarmings, birthdays and thank-yous. — Laila ElGohary

Keys that come apart
I first bought this Troika Patent keyring in 2013, and I’ve given it as a gift many times since. Each key sits on its own ring that snaps off easily, so removing a single key takes a second. I do it more than I expected: when traveling, walking the dog in the park, or handing a mechanic my car key. — Elizabeth Craig

Sticker scraper
The Scotty Peeler is a little scraper with a thin, precise edge that slips under stubborn stickers, labels, tape and adhesive without scratching what’s underneath. I’ve used it on drinking glasses and old window decals. My favorite job was on a vintage domino set from an antique shop in Austin. Some previous owner had covered its plastic case in clear tape, probably decades ago. I only bought the set because I knew my Scotty Peeler was waiting at home. With a little Goo Gone, it came off clean. Not a mark left behind. — Mike Wabschall

Bug vacuum
The BugZooka is a wonderful invention. Simple, sturdy, cheap, no batteries, nothing to wear out, easy to clean and surprisingly powerful. I bought one in 2018 and use it often in the country to suck up bugs, living and dead. I’ve gifted a couple to friends. — Ted

Shower notes
AquaNotes is a waterproof notepad and pencil that stick to the shower wall, ready to catch your deepest shower thoughts, from the day’s to-do list to the eureka moment. Steven Kotler, who writes about peak performance, says showering puts you in a flow state, and AquaNotes turns that time into something you can act on. I buy the bulk pack and keep one in every shower. Tip: stick the pencil to the wall vertically, tip down, so it dries better. — Rusty


Kitchen and Comfort

Throat lozenges for speakers
I speak for a living, and over time my throat has given way. I’ve tried every potion, elixir and emollient, and the one I come back to every time is Grether’s Pastilles. Not a candy, not icky. They simply work. — Seth Godin

Coffee through a straw
The JOGO is a metal drinking straw with a built-in filter and a silicone tip. Dead simple but so useful. I use it daily for coffee: grind beans, add water, stir, brew and drink. Yes, I own pots, cafetières and an AeroPress, but this is the one that gets used every day. It’s also great for tea and maté, and it’s portable for travel. I’m sure coffee experts will tell me why this doesn’t work, but it works for me. — Nigel

My kitchen gadget of the year
The round Dreamfarm Ograte is the best grater I’ve come across since the Microplane. It’s super sharp, easy to clean and easy to store because it’s flat. I hook it over a bowl and grate carrots, cucumber, apples, cheese, chocolate, anything really, then rinse it under the tap and it’s clean. It’s my go-to gift when I’m invited to dinner, alongside a bottle of wine. — Lesley

Flip-flops I can finally wear
I’ve never been able to wear flip-flops because the piece between my toes was always uncomfortable, and my plantar fasciitis acts up without arch support. My daughter told me about Archies, a genuinely comfortable flip-flop I can wear all day. They’re pricier than plain flip-flops, but the arch support is molded into the base and I’ve never had any discomfort wearing them for hours. — Linda

A work-from-home uniform
Every workday I wear a white button-up shirt. I work from a home office, and the shirt signals to my kids, my clients and me that I’m at work. At the end of the day I switch into a black tee. Uniqlo’s white Oxford Slim Shirts are the best quality for the price I’ve found anywhere. They’re easy to iron and have no pocket. I own seven, and they make working from home that much easier. — Matt Deakyne


Gadgets and Gear

Radar for your bike
I got back on my bike after a decade off so I could ride my daughter to preschool. The coolest gadget that came out while I was away is bike radar. The Garmin Varia RearVue 820 pairs with a bike computer or a phone app and alerts you to cars behind you, showing how far back they are and how fast they’re coming. I often get the alert several seconds before I hear the car. I now consider it essential safety gear, especially with a giggling toddler sitting in front of me. We live on narrow, twisty roads, so I got this latest version with the widest field of view. — J

3D printing is easy now
I’ve checked in on 3D printing a few times over the last 15 years, and I somehow missed that it’s now super reliable, easy and fairly inexpensive. Bambu Lab is like the DJI drone of this world, the breakthrough solution. Their A1 Mini is $249, and the P2S is still under $1,000. I’m now building so much I might need a second printer. — Adam Davidson

The stroller that never gets gate-checked
The GB Pockit Air All-Terrain stroller has been our family’s one irreplaceable travel essential, for two kids over five years. It fits under the seat or in the overhead bin, so you never have to gate-check it, and strollers don’t count toward your carry-on limit. When you land, you cruise past everyone waiting for their strollers, a lifesaver on tight connections. I can fold and unfold it while walking, and it’s a tank. Ours has survived European cobblestones and dodged street cats in Istanbul. Most kid products have a reasonable substitute. This one doesn’t. — Jason

Crib sheets that zip on
QuickZip sheets zip onto a crib or toddler bed mattress. They changed our lives when we had a baby with reflux who was constantly spitting up in bed. Changing a crib sheet in the middle of the night is the worst, and with these you just unzip the top layer without lifting the mattress. We still use them for our toddler and give them to all new parents. — Stacey C

Headlamp on the headrest
I keep a headlamp strapped to my driver’s seat headrest. Whenever I’m driving at night, I know exactly where it is when I need to get out in a dark or unlit place. — Qarlos


Apps and Websites

Shared household lists
AnyList lets you make shared lists and streamlines household list-making like nothing else. We keep a running grocery list, plus lists for movie night ideas, hardware store needs and prep for big days out. Knowing everything is shared removes so much mental load. Either of us can add something the moment we think of it (take note, fellow ADHD households), and no one misses a last-minute request. Cell service is spotty where I live, but the list still updates in almost real time when we divide and conquer at a big store. — Claudia C

Making the invisible visible
One of NASA’s hidden treasures is the Scientific Visualization Studio, a vast, searchable collection of visualizations and animations of ocean currents, the changing Earth, solar storms, distant planets and the universe beyond. Many are built directly from scientific data, and they still astonish me. I had a front-row seat to this work for decades as an executive producer at NASA Goddard, and I consider it one of science communication’s great underappreciated resources. It’s also a secret watering hole for documentary makers, with downloadable, production-quality imagery. — Wade Sisler

Books and Podcasts

Prisoners’ Inventions
On my first visit to Arcana Books on the Arts in Culver City, I spotted this book on my way out and bought all four copies to give as holiday gifts. In Prisoners’ Inventions, Angelo, an incarcerated artist in California, draws and describes the contraptions he and his cellmates made. His meticulous ballpoint diagrams show how to make a grilled cheese in a locker, chess pieces from papier-mâché toilet paper and a “stinger” water heater from razor blades, a plastic lid and earphone wire. It celebrates the ingenuity in all of us and is a reminder that creativity often comes from lack, not abundance. — Rusty Blazenhoff

I’m Starting to Worry About This Black Box of Doom
This is really hard. If I tell you Jason Pargin’s I’m Starting to Worry About This Black Box of Doom is the smartest social commentary I’ve read in years, you won’t know how laugh-out-loud funny it is. If I tell you it’s a spirited rebuttal to the doom-laden firehose of newsfeeds and social media, you might expect something sappy or preachy. If I tell you it’s a wildly entertaining thriller, you’ll miss the trick Pargin pulls off: getting you to empathize with the very characters you once abhorred. You’d better just read it. Preferably the audiobook, narrated by Ari Fliakos. — MM Hynes

Stories that put you to sleep
Nothing Much Happens is a podcast of soothing, gentle bedtime stories for grown-ups that stop your mind from spinning. Even when I think I want to hear the whole story, I drop off and never find out what happens. Probably nothing much. — Lisa

The One You Feed
If I could listen to only one podcast, The One You Feed would be it. Eric Zimmer talks with a wide variety of experts about psychology, well-being and personal growth, and he respects my time as a listener. It’s free everywhere, and the ad-free Patreon costs less than a single therapy session. — Kristen Langhoff Grannan

issues.title: Roads / Cardboard Construction Toys / Quick fix for leaks
issues.html:
Projective road cards

This year I stayed at an Airbnb owned by a therapist and discovered Roads, a deck of 67 projective cards that therapists use to help clients picture where they are in life and where they want to go. Each card shows an illustrated path or road, and there are many ways to use them. You can pick one for a new direction you’d like to take, or lay out several to map your journey from where you are now to where you hope to be. Either way, the images start speaking for your inner landscape. It’s made for therapy, but I bought a deck for my own solo reflection. While searching for it, I also found Play Therapy Supply, which seems like a great source for introspective tools even if you’re not a play therapist. — CD

Cardboard Construction Toys

In my experience the greatest toys for kids are large sheets of cardboard from recycled oversized boxes. It’s free. With the addition of a few plastic screws you or the kids can make endless forts, fantasy structures and even costumes by cobbling the cardboard together. The screws I use have a hex head that fits a socket driver or screwdriver. You make a hole with an awl and then hand drive the screw in. Easy and safe for kids to do. The screws are easy to extract and re-use in the next project. A set of Kizzikids 160 screws with 2 drivers ($20) will have more pieces than you’ll ever need – but perfect for a school or camp. Or, if you have a 3D printer you can print Cardboard Fasteners yourself. — KK

Quick fix for leaks

I used Iron Grip self-fusing silicone tape to temporarily patch a leaky hose on my car. To activate it, stretch the tape, then wrap it tightly around a leaky pipe, hose, or wire. It’s great to have some around for plumbing leaks when they happen. You can also wrap it around tool handles for a more comfortable grip. I used the Iron Grip brand, but many other brands are available, and I imagine they’re all pretty much the same. — MF

Charity Navigator

Tis the season to remember the power of philanthropy. Small gifts, well aimed, can make significant impacts. When we are evaluating new-to-us charitable orgs, we use Charity Navigator to assess their reputation, how responsible and transparent they are with their finances. If you are trying to compare global health programs in terms of how many lives are saved or improved per dollar, try GiveWell. If you want to improve the world by supporting art, do your own thing, but do it generously. There are few pleasures as lasting as giving. — KK

Natural hazards by address

If you live in California, MyHazards is a good place to find out which natural hazards you're most susceptible to. Type in your address, city, or ZIP code, and it shows whether you're near earthquake, flood, fire, or tsunami risk, along with practical steps to prepare for each one. I looked up my own address because of all the El Niño talk and learned I'm not in a flood zone, but I am in an earthquake liquefaction zone. It's free and run by the state's Office of Emergency Services. — CD

1,700 free university courses

The Open Culture website maintains a directory of about 1,700 free online courses from top universities like Yale, MIT, Harvard, and Oxford. They are organized by category. Courses include literature, history, philosophy, religion, computer science, physics, biology, economics, psychology, engineering, and more. The courses are offered in audio, video, and text, and none of them require signing up or payment. It’s like a free university you can dip into anytime you want, or a good way to try out a subject before enrolling in a class. Open Culture also has free movies, ebooks, and art images. — MF

issues.title: Design Prompts / RetroCodex / Sunshine Atlas
issues.html:
Design Prompts

This year I manufactured Design Prompts, a box of 110 double-sided cards to help creative people get unstuck. They are inspired by Brian Eno’s Oblique Strategies, but the 216 prompts here are all my own, and more general purpose. And the beautiful box I made for them is much easier to use and store. Magnetic cover, upright stance. Draw a card at random and try what it suggests: “Find the third side” or “Change what you’re optimizing.” Hundreds more. It’s for artists, writers, designers, makers, inventors, and other innovators. Limited edition: only 400 copies, available on Amazon. I use mine all the time. — KK

Update your outdated facts

When you’re young, you learn facts about the world that are later debunked or revised. If you’re curious to see what has changed since you graduated from high school, check out RetroCodex. I learned that Tyrannosaurus rex probably had lips that covered its teeth, that adults can indeed grow new brain cells, that the appendix might actually have a purpose, and that eating eggs won’t raise your blood cholesterol. It also corrected many other facts I was taught the opposite of. It’s a fun way to update your out-of-date mental factbook. — MF

Where the sun is

I don’t like to travel during the winter, but I do like fantasizing about where I could go that’s warm and sunny, so I think Sunshine Atlas is a really cool idea. Pick a month, and the map ranks places around the world by how warm, dry, and sunny they tend to be. It has more parameters and filters than I need, but as a way to chase the sun, it works. Every destination has its own airport, so everything on the map is somewhere you can actually fly. — CD

Posca pens for painting rocks

Kevin has already recommended Posca markers here, but I want to add my own endorsement of these water-based acrylic paint pens. I like to paint on small rocks and have experimented with all kinds of acrylics and gouaches. But as soon as I tried Posca pens, I realized they are superior to a paintbrush. The colors are opaque and vibrant, and I have much more control with a pen nib than with a brush. They work on many surfaces besides rocks, too, including wood, glass, metal, ceramic, and fabric. They come in a range of tip sizes, from extra-fine to broad. — MF

Optimistic adventures

There are a lot of folks vlogging their adventures on YouTube, and you get to travel with them vicariously. Only a few are people I would actually want to spend time with. One guy who makes me happy is Matt Spears. He does stunts like riding a jet ski 1,000 miles to Alaska, or seeing how far he can get on a motorcycle chopper bought on Amazon, and so forth. Things are constantly falling apart, but he is constantly chipper, upbeat, confident, excited, enthusiastic, and his optimism is contagious. I’ll tag along wherever he wants to go. — KK

Live guided imagery journey

A while back I recommended the Pearl Dive, a 30-minute guided imagery journey I listen to whenever I feel confusion or resistance in my body. Dr. Rosalind Watts created it to prepare participants for a clinical trial of psilocybin for depression. It guides you out of your thoughts and down into your body, where buried emotions and desires are waiting. I always discover something new, and when I stay with what feels uncomfortable, it so often becomes a pearl of insight. I’m sharing it again because in a few days Dr. Watts is leading the dive live in a free Zoom session (no psychedelics involved), open to anyone preparing to explore altered states or simply wanting to go deeper into their own experience. Full disclosure, I’m a facilitator with her community, ACER Integration, but being guided through this practice by its creator, for free and in community, feels like a rare gift. The session is Wednesday, November 11, from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. UK time. You can learn more and register for free here. — CD
